terms.definition: multiply each input by its own number (its weight), then add the results up.
the number a model multiplies one feature by. In this chapter the weights are θ₁, θ₂, … θₙ.
θ₀, the constant added to every prediction whatever the inputs are; also called the intercept. (Lesson b08 uses "bias" for something else: an error from wrong assumptions.)
another name for the bias term θ₀: the prediction when every feature is 0.
θ ("theta") is the Greek letter the book uses for the model's numbers: θ₀ is the bias term, θ₁ to θₙ are the weights. Bold θ, or θ written alone, means all of them as one list.
a number inside the model that training chooses: here the θ values.
the model's output for one row, written ŷ ("y hat").
ŷ, the model's prediction; plain y is the true value.
multiply two equal-length lists position by position, then add up the results: [2, 3]·[1, 4] = 2×1 + 3×4 = 14.
turn a grid on its side: rows become columns. Written with a small raised T, e.g. Xᵀ.
a grid of numbers with rows and columns. X, the training data with one row per instance, is a matrix.
mean squared error: square every error (prediction minus truth), then average them. RMSE is its square root.
the single number that says how badly a model's current θ fits the training data; training pushes it down. For linear regression it is the MSE.
the book's old name for the model; that is why it is written h.
a list of numbers written as one column (rows × 1), the shape NumPy code often needs.
an answer computed by one fixed formula in one pass, with no loop and no search.
the closed-form formula θ = (XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀy that gives linear regression's best θ in one step (Equation 4-4).
the matrix version of dividing: a matrix times its inverse changes nothing. Not every matrix has one; a matrix that does is invertible.
a matrix with no inverse.
singular value decomposition: splitting a matrix into three simpler ones. Scikit-Learn uses it to solve linear regression safely.
a stand-in for the inverse that exists even when the true inverse does not.
fitting by making the sum of squared errors as small as possible; linear regression's usual method.
made up by a program on purpose, not collected from the real world.
the random wobble added to each point, the part of y that no rule could predict.
"big O" notation: how the running time grows with the number of features n (or rows m). O(n²) means twice the features, about four times the time.
Scikit-Learn helper that puts a column of 1s in front of every row, so the bias term can be multiplied like any weight.
training by repeated small steps: measure which way the cost goes down fastest, move θ a little that way, repeat.
η ("eta"): how big each gradient-descent step is. Too small is slow; too large overshoots and diverges.
a setting YOU choose before training, such as the learning rate; training never changes it.
settle on (reach) the answer as the steps go on.
get further from the answer with every step, until the numbers blow up.
shaped like one bowl: a single lowest point and no other dips, so walking downhill always reaches it.
a dip that is lower than everything near it but higher than the true lowest point (the global minimum).
the lowest point of the whole cost surface: the best θ.
a nearly flat stretch: steps there are tiny, so progress almost stops. A curve that levels off is also said to plateau.
a line joining points of equal height, as on a map; here, all the θ values that give the same cost.
the slope of the cost in one weight's direction: how fast it changes if you nudge only that weight.
all the partial derivatives stacked into one list; it points uphill, toward a higher cost.
∇, the upside-down triangle: "the gradient of".
one full pass over the training data.
gradient descent that uses the whole training set for every step. ("Batch" here means all the rows, not a chunk of them.)
gradient descent that uses one random row for each step: cheap and fast, but noisy.
random.
a rule that shrinks the learning rate as training goes on.
independent and identically distributed: each row drawn looks like a fair sample of the whole dataset, unrelated to the rows before it.
a small random group of rows (e.g. 20) used for one gradient-descent step.
a graphics chip; it does many multiplications at once, which makes matrix arithmetic fast.
training on data too big for memory by loading one part at a time.
a plot with one axis per model parameter; each point is one candidate θ.
the starting number of the random generator (`np.random.seed(42)`, or `random_state=42` in Scikit-Learn): the same seed gives the same "random" numbers every run.
linear regression fed powers of the inputs (x², x³, …) as extra columns, so it can fit curves.
Scikit-Learn's tool that adds the power and product columns to the data.
the highest power used: degree 2 adds x², degree 10 goes up to x¹⁰.
a formula of the form ax² + bx + c; its graph is a U-shaped curve with one bend.
the prediction is still a plain weighted sum of the columns it is given, even if some columns are x² or x³.
an effect that depends on two inputs together: the effect of a changes with the value of b.
growing by counting every possible combination, which gets big very fast.
a plot of training error and validation error against the number of training rows (or against training time).
how wrong the model is on the rows it learned from.
how wrong the model is on held-out rows it did not learn from.
error from wrong assumptions, such as fitting a straight line to curved data; too much of it is underfitting. Not the same word as the bias term θ₀.
error from a model reacting too much to the exact training rows it saw; too much of it is overfitting.
the part of the error that comes from noise in the data itself; no model can remove it.
how many independent numbers the model can adjust, roughly its number of parameters.
NumPy function: np.linspace(a, b, n) gives n evenly spaced numbers from a to b.
linear regression plus a penalty on the sum of the squared weights, so the weights stay small.
α, the regularization strength: 0 means no penalty; larger means a stronger pull on the weights toward 0.
an extra amount added to the cost to discourage something, here large weights.
a square matrix with 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere; multiplying by it changes nothing.
a matrix factorisation, like SVD, that Ridge can use to compute the closed-form answer quickly.
two ways to measure the size of a list of weights: ℓ1 adds their sizes (signs dropped), ℓ2 adds their squares. Ridge uses ℓ2, lasso ℓ1.
linear regression plus a penalty on the sum of the weights' sizes (signs dropped); it pushes useless weights to exactly 0.
a number's size without its minus sign: the absolute value of −3 is 3.
mostly zeros: a sparse model has most of its weights exactly 0.
keeping only the useful input columns and dropping the rest.
a stand-in for the gradient at a sharp corner, where the true slope does not exist.
sign(x) is −1 for a negative number, +1 for a positive one, 0 for zero.
two columns are correlated when they tend to move together, so they carry much the same information.
linear regression with both the ridge and the lasso penalty at once, mixed by a ratio r.
r in elastic net (l1_ratio in Scikit-Learn): the share of the penalty that is lasso's; the rest is ridge's.
easy to read: you can see which features the model actually uses.
regularizing by stopping training at the epoch where the validation error was lowest.
a full, independent copy of an object and everything inside it; later changes to the original do not reach it.
Scikit-Learn call that trains one more epoch, continuing from where the model already is (plain fit would start from scratch).
in early stopping: how many epochs without improvement to wait before stopping.
a model that answers a yes/no question instead of predicting a number (lesson b13 explains how).
a model built from many small connected units, the subject of Chapter 10 onward.
how likely something is, from 0 (never) to 1 (certain).
σ(t) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᵗ), also called the logistic function: it squeezes any number into the range 0 to 1, and σ(0) = 0.5.
e raised to a power, eˣ, where e ≈ 2.718; always positive, and it grows very fast.
the class labelled 1 (the yes answer); the negative class is labelled 0. Neither word means good or bad.
the cut-off that turns a probability into a yes/no answer; 0.5 by default.
another word for the cost: the error score that training makes as small as it can; the book tends to say "loss" for that number while training is running.
logistic regression's cost function: the average of −log(the probability the model gave the correct answer).
the inputs where the model's probability is exactly 50%: on one side it answers yes, on the other no.
a flower. The iris dataset: 150 flowers of three species (setosa, versicolor, virginica), each with 4 measurements in cm.
petals are the inner, upright parts of a flower; sepals are the outer parts underneath.
a plot with one axis per feature, where each flower is one dot.
Scikit-Learn function that splits rows at random into a training set and a test set (25% test unless told otherwise).
logistic regression for several classes at once: one score per class, turned into probabilities that add up to 1.
the position of the largest value, not the value itself: argmax of [0.1, 0.7, 0.2] is 1.
softmax regression's cost function: the average of −log(the probability given to the correct class). With two classes it is the log loss.
LogisticRegression's regularization setting, the other way round from α: a larger C means weaker regularization.
only one can be true at a time, like a flower's species.
